content.title: About
content.content: Butter in stick form (usually 200 g) is a solid block of pure butter packaged in a convenient rectangular shape. It is made from cow’s milk cream that has been churned into a smooth, creamy mass. The butter has a characteristic milky aroma, a gentle taste and a soft texture suitable for cooking as well as spreading.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally butter was divided into “soft” and “hard” – the stick belongs to the soft category because it slices easily.
In European culinary schools a stick is often used as a precise measure of butter (approximately 1 Tbsp ≈ 14 g).
Butter typically contains about 80 % fat, with the remaining 20 % being water and milk proteins.
Stored in the refrigerator, a butter stick stays fresh for up to 3 weeks; in the freezer it can last up to 6 months.
In some countries (e.g., Japan) butter sticks are sold in individual salted or herb‑flavored packages.

items.title: Source of fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Butter is rich in vitamins A, D, E and K2, which support vision, immunity, skin health and bone metabolism.

items.title: Contains conjugated linoleic acid (CLA)
items.content: CLA may help maintain normal blood sugar levels and has antioxidant properties.

items.title: Supports gut health
items.content: Small amounts of short‑chain fatty acids in butter can promote the growth of beneficial gut bacteria.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The fats in butter are quickly absorbed, providing sustained satiety.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: The fatty matrix of butter enhances the absorption of other fat‑soluble nutrients in a meal.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Excessive intake of saturated fat may raise LDL‑cholesterol, so moderation is recommended.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Butter contains trace amounts of lactose; people with severe intolerance should limit consumption.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein present in butter.

items.title: Oxidation if stored improperly
items.content: When kept at high temperatures butter can become rancid, affecting flavor and aroma.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: A butter stick is easy to slice for spreading on bread, adding to sauces, baking, or sautéing vegetables and meat. It can be melted for flavorful dressings or incorporated into dough for a softer crumb.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store butter in the refrigerator in its original wrapper or an airtight container. For longer storage (over 1 month) it can be frozen, wrapped tightly in plastic. Before use, check the smell – rancid butter has a sharp, unpleasant odor.

chicken-or-turkey-rice-and-vegetables-in.title: Chicken or Turkey with Rice and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of tender chicken or turkey meat, boiled rice, and a mix of vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. It is seasoned with soy‑based sauce, giving it a savory, slightly salty flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are excellent sources of lean protein.
Rice is one of the world’s most consumed grains and provides complex carbohydrates for sustained energy.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and compounds that support detoxification.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables like spinach or kale contain high levels of iron and folate.
Soy sauce originated in China over 2,500 years ago and is now a staple in many Asian cuisines.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Poultry meat supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides glucose, helping maintain energy levels throughout the day.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables add vitamins A, C, K, as well as potassium and magnesium, supporting heart and nerve function.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Skinless poultry contains little saturated fat, making the dish suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Probiotic effect of soy sauce
items.content: Fermented soy sauce contains beneficial microbes that can aid gut microbiota balance.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is high in sodium; people with hypertension should limit its use.

items.title: Pathogens in undercooked poultry
items.content: Insufficiently cooked meat may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

items.title: Portion control for rice
items.content: Large servings of rice can raise blood glucose levels in people with diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot; it pairs well with extra seasonings such as ginger or garlic. Vegetables can be steamed or lightly sautéed to retain crunch and nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to a boil before consuming to eliminate any bacteria.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple, frozen is ripe pineapple that has been quickly frozen after harvest to preserve its flavor, aroma, and nutrients. It is convenient for long‑term storage and culinary use.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple is the only edible fruit of the bromeliad family.
Flash freezing retains more than 90 % of the vitamin C found in fresh pineapple.
Pineapple contains bromelain – an enzyme that helps break down proteins.
Tropical plants like pineapple can thrive in nutrient‑poor soils thanks to symbiotic microbes.
Frozen pineapple is commonly used in smoothies, desserts, and Asian dishes.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain improves digestion and may reduce inflammation.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Pineapple is low in fat and calories, making it a good choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of manganese
items.content: Manganese is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes gut health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Bromelain allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to bromelain, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Pineapple contains natural sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Ice crystal formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to large ice crystals, affecting texture.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Frozen pineapple can be added to smoothies, cocktails, ice cream, baked goods, sauces, and salads. It is usually thawed in the refrigerator or at room temperature before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight bag or container in the freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 2–3 days and do not refreeze.

potato-baked-peel-eaten-with-cheese.title: Potato, baked, peel eaten, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Baked potato with the peel left on and cheese is a popular dish that combines the tender interior of a baked tuber, the flavorful crisp of the skin, and melted cheese. The peel retains most of the nutrients, while the cheese adds protein and a rich taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato skin contains more fiber, vitamin C, and potassium than the flesh alone.
Baking preserves more antioxidants than boiling.
Cheeses commonly used are high‑calcium varieties such as cheddar or parmesan.
In many cuisines the baked potato is seasoned with herbs like rosemary or thyme for extra aroma.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed root vegetables, with over 350 million tonnes produced annually.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The skin provides a substantial amount of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in the skin helps boost immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Baked potatoes release glucose slowly, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Potatoes contain carotenoids and phenolic compounds that combat free radicals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to cheese, especially if it contains lactose.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cheese adds calories and saturated fat; portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese is often salty; people with hypertension should choose low‑salt options.

items.title: Salt on the skin
items.content: The peel is frequently seasoned with salt before baking; excess sodium may be undesirable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wash the potatoes, leave the skin on, cut them in half, brush with olive oil, sprinkle grated cheese, and bake until the cheese is golden and the skin is crisp. Serve hot, optionally topped with herbs or a dollop of sour cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw potatoes in a cool, dark place. Keep the cooked baked potatoes in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. When reheating, add a little oil to restore the crispness of the skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Soft pretzels without gluten are coated with a cinnamon‑sugar blend, giving them a sweet‑spicy flavor. They are made from gluten‑free flour, making them suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. The pretzels have a tender, slightly chewy interior and a fragrant, lightly crisp crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free pretzels let those with celiac disease enjoy a classic snack.
Cinnamon is rich in antioxidants and has been used in baked goods for centuries.
The sugar coating helps keep the crust slightly crisp even on a soft base.
Soft pretzels are often served as a dessert or snack at fairs and cafés.
The cinnamon‑sugar combo enhances aroma, making the treat more aromatic.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Gluten‑free flours and whole‑grain ingredients provide dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cinnamon supplies polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Gluten‑free alternatives often have a lower glycemic index than traditional wheat flour.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates in pretzels quickly supply the body with energy, making them a convenient snack.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or those following a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The product may contain nuts, soy, or dairy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sugar coating adds calories, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Additive considerations
items.content: Some gluten‑free blends include additives that may not be suitable for certain sensitivities.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Soft pretzels can pose a choking risk for young children; supervise their consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzels can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, paired with yogurt or ice cream, or used in dessert platters. Lightly warming them in the oven can intensify the cinnamon aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep refrigerated to maintain softness and prevent drying out. Discard any pretzels that show signs of mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Rabbit meat is tender, light-colored meat with a mild, neutral flavor and very little fat. Raw rabbit meat is sold as whole carcasses or cut into pieces: hind legs, saddle, and front legs. Rabbit is stewed, roasted, and fried in the dishes of many European, Russian, and Central Asian cuisines. It must not be eaten raw.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rabbit meat is white, tender, and contains very little fat.
Rabbit is stewed in sour cream, wine, or mustard and cooked with vegetables and herbs in the cuisines of France, Italy, Russia, and other countries.
Eating only very lean meat such as rabbit, without fat or carbohydrates, can lead to rabbit starvation, a serious metabolic problem caused by too much protein.
Carcasses are sold whole or cut into hind legs, saddle, and front legs.
The saddle (loin) is the most tender part, while the legs are tougher and suited to braising.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Rabbit provides high-quality protein.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is important for the nervous system and the formation of blood cells.

items.title: Contains niacin
items.content: Niacin (vitamin B3) helps the body get energy from food.

items.title: Contains selenium and phosphorus
items.content: Selenium is an antioxidant trace mineral, and phosphorus is needed for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rabbit contains noticeably less fat than many other types of meat.

items.title: Raw meat
items.content: Raw meat may contain Salmonella and Campylobacter; rabbit should be cooked to at least 71 °C (160 °F) inside.

items.title: Wild rabbits
items.content: Wild rabbits and hares can be a source of tularemia, so they should be handled with gloves and cooked thoroughly.

items.title: Rabbit starvation
items.content: Lean meat should be combined with fats and other foods rather than eaten as the only source of nutrition.

items.title: Cross-contamination
items.content: Raw meat and its juices should not come into contact with cooked food, cutting boards, and dishes without washing.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marinate rabbit or stew it right away in sour cream, wine, tomatoes, or mustard, roast it with vegetables and herbs, or brown the pieces and then finish cooking. Lean meat dries out easily, so do not overcook it, and add fat or sauce. Cook to at least 71 °C (160 °F) inside.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw rabbit in the refrigerator in a covered container for no more than one to two days, or freeze it. Thaw in the refrigerator. Keep cooked meat in the refrigerator for three to four days.

rice-brown-with-peas-and-carrots-no-adde.title: Brown Rice with Peas and Carrots, No Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ. This version is prepared with peas and carrots without any added fat, making it a low‑calorie, nutrient‑dense dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice provides more fiber and B‑vitamins than white rice.
Peas are a good source of plant protein and vitamin C.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Cooking without added fat preserves the natural flavors and reduces calorie count.
Such combinations are traditional in Asian cuisines for balanced meals.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Plant‑based protein source
items.content: Peas add a complete set of amino acids beneficial for muscle and tissue health.

items.title: Supports vision
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots is converted to vitamin A, essential for eye health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes the dish suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Rice and peas provide magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, important for overall body function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Brown rice contains phytic acid, which can reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: Despite its fiber, rice can still raise blood sugar levels in diabetics; pairing with protein or fat is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish or a main meal. It reheats well in the microwave or on the stovetop, and can be flavored with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared product in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. It can be frozen for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned spinach consists of cooked spinach leaves that have been heat‑treated and sealed in a jar with added fat. The product is ready to eat, retains most of its nutrients, and has a soft, tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach belongs to the Amaranthaceae family and is grown in temperate climates worldwide.
Canning allows spinach to be stored for several years without loss of flavor.
Added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Spinach is a staple in Mediterranean cuisine, often appearing in casseroles, pastas, and dips.
Many canned spinach products are labeled “no added salt” when salt is omitted.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, immune function, and skin integrity.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron is needed for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes normal digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients in spinach help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If salt is added, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Leaf‑vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to spinach.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Spinach contains oxalates, which can contribute to kidney‑stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned spinach can be eaten cold in salads, added to soups, stews, pasta dishes, or used as a filling for pies and quiches. Shake the jar before opening to distribute the fat evenly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the spinach in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet potato (batata) is a starchy root vegetable rich in carbohydrates, vitamins, and minerals. Boiling retains most of its nutrients, and adding a modest amount of fat (oil or butter) enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins and makes the dish more satiating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sweet potato belongs to the Convolvulaceae family and is not related to regular potato.
There are over 600 cultivars, varying in flesh color from white to bright orange and purple.
Orange-fleshed varieties are high in beta‑carotene, a provitamin A that the body converts to vitamin A.
Batata is a staple in traditional dishes across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean.
Boiling in the skin preserves more fiber and nutrients than peeling beforehand.

items.title: Rich in beta‑carotene
items.content: Orange sweet potato provides a high amount of provitamin A, supporting vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates deliver a steady release of glucose, helping maintain energy levels and satiety.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes a healthy gut microbiome, and helps regulate cholesterol.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sweet potato supplies vitamin B6, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides potassium, magnesium, and iron, important for heart, muscle, and blood health.

items.title: High glycemic response without fat
items.content: When eaten without added fat, sweet potato can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be a concern for people with diabetes.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals allergic to other nightshade family plants may react to sweet potato.

items.title: Watch added fat quantity
items.content: Excessive oil or butter increases calorie density and can contribute to weight gain.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled sweet potato can be served as a side dish, added to salads, mashed, or blended into soups. For optimal vitamin A and E absorption, drizzle a small amount of olive oil, butter, or nut oil over the cooked product.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep boiled sweet potato in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze portioned pieces—they retain flavor and nutrients.
